results.authors: Prabhakaran S, Gonzalez NR, Zachrison KS, et al.
results.key_finding: IV thrombolysis with alteplase 0.9 mg/kg or tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg is recommended within 4.5 hours of last known well, with blood pressure below 185/110 mmHg before treatment; thrombectomy is recommended for anterior circulation large vessel occlusion within 6 hours with NIHSS 6 or more and ASPECTS 3 to 10, and selected patients up to 24 hours by DAWN or DEFUSE 3 criteria.
results.title: 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke

results.authors: Nogueira RG, Jadhav AP, Haussen DC, et al.
results.key_finding: In patients with LVO presenting 6-24 hours after last known well with clinical-core mismatch, thrombectomy led to better functional outcomes at 90 days versus standard care.
results.title: Thrombectomy 6-24 hours after stroke with a mismatch between deficit and infarct (DAWN)

results.authors: Albers GW, Marks MP, Kemp S, et al.
results.key_finding: Thrombectomy in patients with LVO 6-16 hours after symptom onset selected by perfusion imaging mismatch criteria significantly improved functional outcomes.
results.title: Thrombectomy for Stroke at 6 to 16 Hours (DEFUSE 3)

results.authors: Adams HP Jr, Bendixen BH, Kappelle LJ, et al.
results.key_finding: TOAST classification categorizes ischemic stroke into large-artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolism, small-vessel occlusion, other determined etiology, and undetermined. Cardioembolic strokes are associated with cardiac sources including atrial fibrillation.

Do not delay thrombectomy to observe the response to IV thrombolysis.

required_recommendations: Establish last known well (09:00, 2 hours 58 minutes before arrival) and the NIHSS (13).

IV thrombolysis: give once blood pressure is below 185/110 mmHg (2 hours 58 minutes from last known well, no anticoagulant, INR 1.0, platelets 231, glucose 138 mg/dL, no haemorrhage). Thrombectomy: proceed for the right M1 occlusion (NIHSS 13, living independently before the stroke, ASPECTS 8, within 6 hours); do not wait for the response to thrombolysis.
Achieve a door-to-needle time under 60 minutes.

Lower blood pressure below 185/110 mmHg (188/104 on arrival) with IV labetalol or nicardipine before IV thrombolysis, then keep it below 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours; after successful recanalization do not target systolic blood pressure below 140 mmHg.
Monitor closely for orolingual angioedema during and after thrombolysis (she takes lisinopril, an ACE inhibitor).
Verify glucose to exclude hypoglycemia as a stroke mimic (glucose mildly elevated, not hypoglycemic)
Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours.

Start apixaban 5 mg twice daily for the newly found atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc 6; HAS-BLED 3 for this stroke, age over 65 and aspirin) on day 6 to 7, because the infarct is major by ELAN imaging criteria (cortical and deep MCA branches), once follow-up imaging excludes haemorrhagic transformation; do not bridge with heparin, and stop aspirin when apixaban starts.

Atrial fibrillation on the initial ECG with a large cortical and deep right MCA infarct and a right M1 occlusion establishes a cardioembolic mechanism by TOAST; carotid stenosis under 30% on CTA excludes large-artery atherosclerosis as a competing mechanism

Last known well 2 hours 58 minutes before arrival: within the 4.5-hour IV thrombolysis window; the right M1 occlusion with NIHSS 13 and ASPECTS 8 meets the 0 to 6 hour thrombectomy criteria (AHA/ASA 2026, COR 1), with IV thrombolysis first

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Dorothy Harrington is a 74-year-old right-handed woman with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes who was brought to the emergency department by her daughter after sudden onset of left-sided weakness and behavioral change. The daughter reports she called her mother at approximately 09:00 this morning and she sounded entirely normal. She arrived at her mother's home at 11:20 for a planned visit and found her sitting in the kitchen chair unable to rise, with her left arm hanging limply at her side and appearing oblivious to objects and people on her left side. The patient denied anything was wrong when asked, attributing her inability to stand to her bad knees. The daughter called 911 immediately. EMS arrived at 11:34 and documented left hemiplegia, apparent neglect of the left side, and rightward gaze preference. A stroke alert was activated in the field. Blood glucose obtained by EMS was 128 mg/dL. The patient arrived in the emergency department at 11:58. Last known well time is established at 09:00, approximately 2 hours and 58 minutes before ED arrival. On cardiac monitoring in the ED, the rhythm appeared irregularly irregular, prompting an urgent 12-lead ECG. The patient is unable to reliably report symptom onset; she demonstrates apparent anosognosia for her left-sided deficits. She denies headache, nausea, vomiting, or loss of consciousness. She reports no recent chest pain, fever, or illness. Her medications include amlodipine, lisinopril, atorvastatin, and aspirin 81 mg daily. She has not taken any anticoagulants. Her blood pressure on arrival is 188/104 mmHg, which she and her daughter attribute to her chronic hypertension. The daughter confirms her mother has never been diagnosed with atrial fibrillation and has not seen a cardiologist in several years.
